state.case_summary:
A 45-year-old man presented with a three-week history of a tender, slow-growing left axillary lump and a low-grade fever (37.5–38°C) for one week. His medical history was notable for hypertension—treated with lacidipine, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide—and a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass performed two years earlier, after which he lost 112 kg (BMI from 64.6 to 28 kg/m2). He smoked 30 cigarettes daily and took vitamin (A, D, E, B complex), calcium, cholecalciferol, and iron supplements. There was no personal or family history of autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disease.

On examination, he had a tender, non-mobile, 3 × 4 cm lymph node in the left axilla; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including a complete blood count, ESR, liver and renal panels, autoantibodies (ANA, RF), complement levels, inflammatory markers, thyroid function, and serologies for a broad spectrum of viral and parasitic pathogens—were all normal or negative. A thoracoabdominal CT scan was unremarkable except for the axillary lymphadenopathy. A biopsy of the axillary node revealed coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate. An investigation for mycobacteria was negative.
